title: CPI(M) MP John Brittas Dragged and Assaulted by Delhi Police, Then Dumped Roadside
excerpt: The Rajya Sabha MP says he was manhandled inside a police bus despite identifying himself as a parliamentarian, released only after a DCP reviewed body-cam footage; he has written to the President and CJI seeking an independent investigation.
body:
• Rajya Sabha MP and CPI(M) leader John Brittas says he was dragged roughly 50 metres, lifted bodily into a police bus and assaulted inside it by Delhi Police and CRPF personnel on Sunday, October 11, while speaking to journalists at a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
  • Brittas was released after a deputy commissioner of police reviewed body-camera footage and ordered his release; he was later taken to Delhi's Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital for an X-ray and medical examination.
  • The MP has written to President Droupadi Murmu, the Chief Justice of India and the Rajya Sabha chairman seeking an independent investigation, alleging the incident happened just hours after the Supreme Court directed that peaceful protesters face no unlawful detention.

Rajya Sabha MP and CPI(M) leader John Brittas was allegedly assaulted by Delhi Police and Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) personnel in New Delhi on Sunday, October 11, during an ongoing protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar — an incident that has drawn allegations of police brutality against a sitting parliamentarian.

Brittas says he reached the Connaught Place area around 12:30 p.m. after learning that youth activists were being assaulted and detained, and was speaking to journalists about the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation when security personnel forcibly manhandled him. "I was peacefully exercising my democratic right to speak to the press. Nevertheless, personnel of the Delhi Police and the Central Reserve Police Force forcibly manhandled and dragged me for approximately 50 metres, despite repeated assertions by me and the journalists present that I am a sitting Member of Parliament," Brittas said in his account of the incident, according to LiveLaw. Video footage circulating from the scene appears to show security personnel dragging the MP away mid-interview.

Inside the police vehicle

Brittas alleges the treatment worsened after he was forced into a police bus. Several CRPF personnel pinned him and another person down against a seat, he said, and continued to restrain him despite his repeated identification as a Member of Parliament. "They pinned me to the seat and tried to choke me. This is the plight of an MP in this country," Brittas told the media, per The Hindu. He said he began experiencing breathing difficulties during the ordeal.

https://x.com/cpimspeak/status/2109208597704138855

The situation de-escalated only after a deputy commissioner of police intervened — according to Brittas, the senior officer reviewed body-camera footage, recognised his status as a parliamentarian and ordered his release. The MP was then removed from the vehicle and left by the roadside, where he sat on the pavement struggling to catch his breath before a young man identified as Sajid Hussain helped him find an autorickshaw. He was later admitted to Delhi's Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital, where he underwent an X-ray and a medical examination to check for possible chest injuries. CPI(M) general secretary M.A. Baby and RJD MP Manoj Jha visited him at the hospital, and the CPI(M) shared video of the incident as evidence of what it described as police brutality.

"Manhandled, dragged, assaulted and misbehaved inside a police vehicle and dumped by the roadside — for the crime of speaking to the media."

— John Brittas, Rajya Sabha MP

Why they were protesting: the SIR controversy

The protest Brittas joined is part of a wider agitation over the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls — a door-to-door verification exercise in which booth-level officers re-check voter lists and require documentation from voters, a process opposition parties allege is being used to disenfranchise opposition-leaning voters. The demonstrations, backed by Citizens for Justice and Peace (CJP), entered their second day on Sunday, with police detaining protesters attempting to march toward Jantar Mantar. Earlier coverage by The Videshi reported that the Supreme Court had barred illegal detentions in the Delhi protest case and ordered normal metro and internet operations — a directive Brittas pointedly invoked.

"Brittas emphasized that the incident occurred shortly after the Supreme Court issued directives regarding peaceful protests, stating that unarmed individuals could only be detained under lawful circumstances," Daily Kiran reported. In his letter to the CJI, Brittas has argued that a credible investigation cannot be left to a chain of command whose own personnel may be implicated, and has asked that his complaint be placed before an appropriate Supreme Court Bench for consideration, including possible cognizance or proceedings under Article 32 of the Constitution.

The other side, and what comes next

Delhi Police has not, in the available reports, issued a detailed response to Brittas's specific allegations. What is on record is the MP's own account that a senior officer — the DCP — reviewed the footage and ordered his release after his detention was deemed unlawful, which corroborates that something about the detention went wrong procedurally. News reports also caution that the precise timing and circumstances of the footage shared by the CPI(M) were not independently established. The MP has asked for the preservation of media and public video footage, police duty rosters, wireless logs and all records relating to his detention — evidence that, if preserved, will determine whether the assault inside the police vehicle can be independently verified.

For diaspora readers, the episode is another data point in a tense season of Indian democratic contention: a Supreme Court ruling one day, an alleged assault on a sitting MP the next. The Supreme Court's directions on protest policing, reported earlier by The Videshi, will be the legal yardstick against which both sides' accounts are measured.
